newsitem.title: JAPAN: TCI head says satellite 'bubble' not scary to CATV.
newsitem.headline: TCI head says satellite 'bubble' not scary to CATV.

text.p: Tele-Communications Inc chief John Malone said on Tuesday that cable television (CATV) operators are unfazed by the challenge of digital broadcast satellites.

Malone, president and chief executive officer of TCI, which faces growing competition from direct satellite broadcasting, also predicted that terrestrial optic fibre networks would be the "dominant distribution technology" for broadcasting video and personal computer connections.
"We have learned that the satellite economic bubble is not necessarily as scary to a cable operator as it might appear," Malone told a news conference.
He emphasised satellites' high vulnerability to cost increases in programming due to their large number of channels.

"The break-even point for DirecTV, I'm told, is 4.5 million customers...they are at two to three million today," Malone said, adding that substantial rate increases would be required for it to have any hope of getting break-even at a realistic number.
DirecTV is the satellite television division of Hughes Electronics Inc.
TCI itself ran into some rough spots last year when it raised rates. It saw customers walk into the arms of the new digital broadcast industry.
In December, TCI announced a cost-cutting programme that included layoffs of 2,500 employees, or about 6.5 percent of its work force, salary cuts and freezes for executives.
TCI recently announced it would raise its rates again from June due to high programming costs. TCI now serves 14 million customers.
Malone said TCI is accelerating investment in high-capacity communication networks, shifting the focus more to high-speed data connectivity and the Internet.
"We are changing the architecture...to cope with continuing connectivity by PC and Internet users," Malone said.
Large capacity and interactivity are benefits of terrestrial fibre network systems, he said.
"Once people who use Internet-type of services experience the instantaneous capacity (of fibre networks), you can't get away from it," he said.
A PC modem connecting PCs and cables has yet to be standarised, but TCI hopes the standard will be decided by the end of this year, he said.
But Malone said Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp's project of connecting every Japanese home with fibre networks by the year 2010 is not "efficient".
Malone said laying fibres only to switchboards in residential areas and using coaxial lines for the rest would be more cost-effective.
"But if we could lease from them at less expensive costs we would welcome it," Malone said.
